title: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing
name: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing in Phoenix, AZ
metaDescription: Sourcing multifamily replacement property in metro Phoenix for 1031 exchange investors, from West Valley new construction to older core value-add.

sections.html: Phoenix multifamily is not one market. It's a new-construction growth ring in the West Valley and an older, cheaper core that trades on rent upside. We source in both directions depending on what your exchange needs.

sections.heading: New Supply Chasing the West Valley Rooftops
sections.html:
Goodyear, Surprise, and Buckeye have added apartment stock faster than almost anywhere else in the metro, riding the same population growth that's filling the industrial corridor along Loop 303. That new product trades at tighter cap rates because the buildings are new, the finishes are current, and lenders like the growth story.

If your exchange is size-constrained after a sale, this is often where the debt gets easiest to place, since newer buildings underwrite cleaner than a 1980s deal.

sections.heading: Value-Add in the Older Core
sections.html:
Garden-style Class B and C buildings from the 1970s and 1980s sit through central Phoenix, Glendale, and parts of Mesa. Rents in these buildings often sit below what a renovated unit next door commands, and Arizona has no statewide rent control, so an owner who repositions units can reset rent on turnover without a local cap fighting them.

The tradeoff is older mechanical systems and roofs, plus more hands-on management than a new build.

sections.heading: What We Check Before You Identify a Deal
sections.html:
Every multifamily candidate goes through the same pass before we put it in front of you:

  • Trailing twelve months of income and expenses against current market rent
  • Physical condition of roofs, plumbing, and HVAC, weighted for Phoenix summer wear
  • Insurance quotes, since Arizona premiums have moved up in the last few years
  • Delinquency and concession trends on the current rent roll
  • Local submarket permit activity for competing new supply

That screen catches most of the deals that look good on a broker flyer and fall apart on inspection.

sections.heading: Matching Sourcing to Your Identification Timeline
sections.html:
Multifamily deals in growth submarkets move fast, so we start building a candidate list before your relinquished property closes. Once you're inside the 45-day identification window, your qualified intermediary needs specific addresses in writing, and we want those addresses to already be underwritten, not still on a broker's early list.

We don't advise on tax outcomes. If unit count, price, or debt on the replacement is lower than what you sold, ask your CPA whether that gap creates boot before you sign.

sections.heading: Where This Goes Wrong
sections.html:
The common mistake is chasing a low cap rate in a new-construction submarket without checking how much competing supply is still permitted nearby. We pull permit data for anything within a couple miles before we recommend a deal, because Phoenix approves new apartment projects fast when land is available.

A second mistake is treating every West Valley submarket the same. Goodyear and Surprise absorbed new units at different rates over the last few years, and a building that leases up quickly in one submarket can sit longer in the other simply because of how much competing product delivered at the same time.

sections.heading: How Financing Shifts Between the Two Submarket Types
sections.html:
Lenders treat new-construction West Valley product and older core value-add differently, and that shows up in your exchange planning. Newer buildings with stabilized occupancy and current finishes tend to qualify for more aggressive debt terms, which matters if you're trying to size a replacement loan against sale proceeds from your relinquished property. Older Class B and C buildings often need a business plan attached, renovation scope, projected rent bumps, timeline, before a lender will commit to similar terms.

We flag which financing path a candidate property fits before you identify it, so your lender conversation starts with the right expectations instead of a mismatch discovered midway through underwriting.

sections.heading: A Note on Insurance Across Both Submarket Types
sections.html: Newer West Valley buildings generally quote lower on insurance than older central Phoenix stock, partly because of updated roofing, plumbing, and electrical systems that reduce claim risk. That gap has widened as Arizona premiums have climbed overall, so we always get a current quote on older buildings before assuming a deal's expense line still matches what the seller has been paying.

faqs.q: Is West Valley new construction or central Phoenix value-add the better 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: It depends on your goals. New construction underwrites cleaner and finances easier; older Class B and C buildings offer rent upside since Arizona has no rent control. We source both and let the numbers make the case.

faqs.q: How does Arizona's lack of rent control affect a multifamily 1031 replacement?
faqs.a: Owners can reset rent to market on turnover without a local rate cap, which is part of why value-add deals in the older core still pencil. That's a market fact, not tax guidance, so run your projections past your own advisor.

faqs.q: What financial records should I see before identifying a multifamily property?
faqs.a: At minimum, trailing twelve months of income and expenses, current rent roll with delinquency and concessions, and recent insurance quotes. We pull all three before a property goes on your short list.

faqs.q: Can I identify more than one multifamily property in my 45-day window?
faqs.a: Yes, subject to whichever identification rule your qualified intermediary is applying to your exchange. We keep a backup candidate ready in case your first choice falls through in diligence.

faqs.q: Why are insurance quotes such a big part of your screening?
faqs.a: Arizona property insurance costs have risen, and a bad quote can quietly wreck a deal's cash flow. We get a real quote before you identify, not after you're locked into the purchase.
